transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?

How I feel about my body and weight is completely controlling how I see myself and how I function at school. I'm an elementary school teacher, and it has gotten to the point where my self-worth is so low that I struggle to even stand in front of my class. I just feel completely overwhelmed by these thoughts and realized I need help.

When you think about your body and weight, is the main problem that you feel overweight or flawed despite reassurance from others, or is it more that you have been feeling persistently depressed and losing interest or enjoyment in most things?

It is definitely about my body and weight, not just a general loss of interest in things. Every morning, looking at the scale and picking myself apart in the mirror completely dictates whether I feel like a success or a total failure for the day. My low mood and why I've been pulling away from social activities are entirely driven by this obsession and feeling so out of control.
Do you ever feel that a specific part of your body is ugly, deformed, or seriously flawed, even when other people say it looks normal?

Yes, absolutely. I stand in front of the mirror every morning picking apart my stomach and thighs, feeling like they look completely wrong and way too big. It makes me feel like a total failure, even though others would probably tell me they look perfectly normal.
Have you ever been significantly underweight, or do you spend a lot of time worrying that you might gain weight and trying to avoid it?

No, I've never been significantly underweight, but I am absolutely terrified of gaining weight and worry about it constantly. If the scale goes up by even a single pound, I feel like a complete failure and will punish myself by skipping meals and over-exercising until I'm lightheaded just to avoid putting on weight.
Have you ever had a period of being significantly underweight, or do you regularly restrict food, skip meals, or exercise mainly to prevent weight gain?

No, I have never been significantly underweight. But I regularly skip breakfast and lunch, and then force myself to jog or do workout videos until I'm shaky and lightheaded to 'make up' for what I ate. It's my way of punishing myself and trying to control my weight after a bad night of overeating.
When you feel you have overeaten, do you ever have episodes where you eat a very large amount of food in a short time while feeling out of control?

Yes, that happens quite often. I'll end up eating an entire frozen pizza, a family-sized bag of chips, and sweets in under an hour. It's like a switch flips and I'm just watching myself from the outside unable to stop, only ending when the food is completely gone and I feel sick and ashamed.
After these binge-eating episodes, do you ever make yourself vomit, use laxatives/diuretics, or fast/exercise specifically to prevent weight gain?

I don't make myself vomit or use laxatives, but I heavily rely on fasting and extreme exercise to compensate. I will skip breakfast and lunch the next day and force myself to jog or do workout videos until I am shaky and lightheaded. I just feel like I don't deserve to stop until I've "earned" back the calories.
After the binge episodes, do you ever vomit, use laxatives or diuretics, or is your compensation mainly fasting and excessive exercise?

No, I never vomit or use things like laxatives or diuretics. My compensation is strictly fasting by skipping breakfast and lunch the next day, and forcing myself to jog or do workout videos until I'm shaky and lightheaded. I just feel like I don't deserve to stop until I've "earned" back the calories.
When you have these binge-eating episodes, do they usually happen at least once a week for several months, or are they less frequent than that?
Yes, they actually happen much more often than that, usually four or five nights a week. This whole pattern of binging and then trying to make up for it has been going on for about four months now.
Have your binge-eating episodes and compensatory behaviors been happening on average at least once a week for the past 3 months, or has it been less frequent than that?

Yes, it has definitely been much more frequent than that, usually happening four or five nights a week. This entire pattern has been going on consistently for about four months now, ever since the pressure at school escalated.
Have you ever had binge-eating episodes without trying to compensate afterward with fasting, skipping meals, or excessive exercise?

No, I almost always feel compelled to compensate after a binge. The guilt and shame are just so overwhelming that I feel like I have to punish myself to "earn back" the calories, so I almost always fast or overexercise the next day instead of just letting it go.
Do you ever make yourself vomit after eating, or use laxatives, diuretics, or diet pills to try to prevent weight gain?

No, I never make myself vomit or use laxatives, diuretics, or diet pills. Instead, my way of compensating is strictly by skipping breakfast and lunch the next day and forcing myself to jog or do workout videos until I'm shaky and lightheaded.
When you binge, do you ever have periods where you eat a very large amount of food but do not try to compensate afterward with fasting or exercise?

No, it is very rare for me to have an episode without trying to make up for it. The guilt and shame are just so overwhelming that I almost always feel compelled to compensate. I'll inevitably punish myself by skipping meals the next day and forcing myself to overexercise to "earn back" the calories.
Do you ever have binge-eating episodes without any compensatory behavior afterward, such as fasting, skipping meals, or excessive exercise?

No, I almost never have a binge without compensating afterward. The guilt and shame are so intense that I feel compelled to punish myself and "earn back" the calories. I almost always follow a blowout by skipping breakfast and lunch the next day and forcing myself to exercise until I'm completely exhausted.

During the times when you binge and then compensate, do you ever have a period of at least 3 months where these episodes happen at least once a week, and have they ever occurred when your weight was significantly low?

Yes, this pattern has been going on for about four months now, usually happening four or five nights a week. However, my weight has never been significantly low; my struggle is really about my intense fear of gaining weight and the distress I feel over my body shape.
Have you ever been significantly underweight, or has your weight generally stayed in the normal or above-normal range?

I'm not entirely sure of my exact weight history, but I don't think I've ever been classified as significantly underweight. My weight has fluctuated over the years, but I believe it has generally stayed within a normal range.
Have you ever been significantly underweight, or has your weight generally stayed in the normal or above-normal range?

As I mentioned, I don't think I've ever been significantly underweight and have generally stayed in the normal weight range. Even though my weight is normal, I have always felt incredibly uncomfortable with my body and how I look.
Have you ever had a period of being significantly underweight, or has your weight generally stayed in the normal or above-normal range?

No, I've never been significantly underweight, and my weight has generally stayed in the normal range. But despite that, I have always felt like I was too big and constantly felt the need to lose weight.
Have you ever been significantly underweight at any point, or has your weight always stayed in the normal or above-normal range?

I don't think I've ever been significantly underweight, though I'm not entirely sure about my exact weight history over the years. Even if my weight has stayed in the normal range, I still constantly struggle with how my body looks and feels every single day.
Have you ever had a period of being significantly underweight, or has your weight generally stayed in the normal or above-normal range?
I believe my weight has generally stayed in the normal range over the years. I don't think I've ever been significantly underweight, though I'm not entirely sure about my exact weight history.
Have you ever been significantly underweight, even for a period of time, or has your weight always stayed in the normal or above-normal range?

I don't believe I've ever been significantly underweight, and my weight has usually stayed in the normal range. Regardless of the actual number, I still spend all my energy obsessing over what the scale says and feeling completely miserable about my body shape.
Have you ever been significantly underweight at any point in your life, even briefly, or has your weight always stayed in the normal or above-normal range?
I don't think I've ever been significantly underweight, but I'm not entirely sure. As far as I know, my weight has always stayed generally within the normal range.
Have you ever been significantly underweight at any point, or has your weight generally stayed in the normal or above-normal range?

I don't think I've ever been significantly underweight, and my weight has generally stayed in the normal range. I'm not entirely sure about my exact weight history over the years, but it has never been very low.
Have you ever had a period of being underweight because of dieting, vomiting, fasting, or excessive exercise, or has your weight generally stayed in the normal range despite these symptoms?

I'm not entirely sure, but I don't think I've ever actually become underweight from doing these things. Despite all the fasting and overexercising, my weight has generally stayed within a relatively normal range.
When you look at your body, is your main distress about your shape and fear of gaining weight, or is it more that you believe a specific body part is defective or deformed despite reassurance?

My main distress is definitely about my overall shape, weight, and the intense fear of gaining weight, rather than thinking a specific body part is deformed. While I do pick apart my stomach and thighs in the mirror, it is completely tied to what the scale says and my fear of putting on weight. That fear is what ultimately dictates how I feel about myself as a whole.
When you think about your body, is your main fear gaining weight and becoming fat, or is it more that you believe a specific body part is ugly or deformed even if your weight stays the same?

My main fear is absolutely gaining weight and becoming fat, and I obsess over the scale to the point where even a single pound increase makes me feel like a complete failure. While I do pick apart my stomach and thighs, it's completely tied to my overall weight and shape rather than seeing them as deformed independent of my weight. That terror of putting on weight is what really controls how I see myself.
When you look at your body, is your distress mainly about your weight and fear of gaining weight, or do you believe a specific body part is ugly or deformed even if your weight stays the same?

It is definitely about my overall weight and shape, and my intense fear of gaining weight. While I do pick apart my stomach and thighs in the mirror, that distress is completely tied to the scale—if it goes up even a single pound, it ruins my day and makes me feel like a complete failure. The number on the scale is what really controls my self-worth, rather than a belief that a specific part is deformed on its own.
When you think about your body, is your distress mainly about your weight and fear of gaining weight, or do you believe a specific body part is ugly or deformed even if your weight stays the same?

It is definitely about my overall weight and shape, which is heavily tied to what the scale says. While I do pick apart my stomach and thighs in the mirror, it's because of my fear of gaining weight, not because I think they are deformed regardless of my weight. If the scale goes up even a single pound, I feel like a complete failure.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets criteria for bulimia nervosa: recurrent binge-eating episodes with loss of control, occurring 4–5 times weekly for about 4 months, followed by inappropriate compensatory behaviors (fasting/skipping meals and excessive exercise). Self-evaluation is strongly influenced by body shape and weight, with intense fear of weight gain. There is no history of significantly low weight, making anorexia nervosa less likely.
